data.title: Course Map and How to Use This Document
data.subtitle: English for Engineering I — Weeks 5–7

narr: Welcome to this comprehensive guide for weeks 5 through 7 of the English for Engineering I course at Tashkent University of Technology. This document serves as your complete companion for the Foundation course, designed to help you transition from general school English to confident, accurate, and organized everyday and academic communication.

The course spans 60 classroom hours—30 lectures and 30 practical sessions—plus 60 hours of independent study. It's mandatory for all Bachelor of Science tracks with no prerequisites or co-requisites. This companion was carefully compiled from every relevant course file for this block, including lecture decks and grammar worksheets.

Each weekly section follows the same structure: first, a rules catalogue with every rule and language box taught that week, numbered for easy reference. Then, questions and tasks grouped exactly as they appear in the source files, each tagged with its source and followed immediately by a complete answer key.

The appendix at the end provides quick-reference materials, including a passive quick reference, a graph language bank, a noun formation table, and revision answers. This ensures the question bank here is complete 'to the end'.

rows.text: Describing Processes and Sequences: grammar — the passive (all tenses); previewed through the TED talk 'The solution to our energy problems... is a toaster'; lecture works through manufacturing-process vocabulary, reading 'How Is Tea Made?', and describing-a-process strand around solar-radiation text and sequencing language.

Understanding Graphs and Short Talks: oral expression — describing simple graphs and charts; TED talk 'How to Spot a Misleading Graph'; cause-and-effect language; listening to short talks — structure and signposting
Comparing Solutions: grammar — noun formation (word formation video 'Virtually Fluent'; suffixes, prefixes, roots, compound nouns, conversion); reading comprehension; oral expression — Switch Games

narr: Let's take a look at the weekly plan for this course block. Week 5 focuses on describing processes and sequences, with the grammar strand being the passive voice in all tenses. This is introduced through a TED talk and reinforced with various activities including vocabulary building and reading comprehension.

Week 6 shifts to understanding graphs and short talks. The oral expression strand trains students to describe simple graphs and charts, while the lecture adds cause-and-effect language and listening skills for analyzing short talks.

Week 7 completes the block with comparing solutions. The grammar strand covers noun formation through various processes, followed by reading comprehension and an oral expression activity called Switch Games.

data.title: Week 5 — Describing Processes and Sequences; the Passive
data.subtitle: Grammar catalogue for Week 5

narr: Now let's dive into Week 5, which focuses on describing processes and sequences, with the primary grammar strand being the passive voice in all tenses. This section collects the language reference panel from the Week 5 lecture and the complete rules page from the Week 5 grammar worksheet.

data.heading: Form of the Passive
bullets: We often use the passive (be + past participle) when it isn't said, known, or important who does an action.

Examples: 'A lot of films are shot on location.' 'The director died when the film was being made.' 'When is our car being repaired?' 'You'll be picked up at the airport by one of our staff.' 'This bill must be paid tomorrow.' 'I love being given a massage.' 'The new concert hall will be opened by the King.'
In passive sentences, the object of the verb becomes the new subject: 'Artem's bike has been stolen.' (Somebody has stolen Artem's bike, but we don't know who.)

narr: The passive voice is formed using the verb 'be' plus the past participle of the main verb. We use this construction when the person performing the action is unknown, unimportant, or when we want to emphasize the object of the action rather than the doer.

For example, in 'A lot of films are shot on location,' the focus is on the films, not on who shot them. Similarly, 'When is our car being repaired?' emphasizes the car being repaired, not who is doing the repairing.

A key characteristic of passive sentences is that the object of the active sentence becomes the new subject. In 'Artem's bike has been stolen,' the bike is now the subject of the sentence, while the person who stole it is not mentioned.

data.heading: Use of the Passive
bullets: (a) To move important information—the object of the active sentence—to the beginning of the sentence: 'Two men are being questioned by the police.'
(b) To be impersonal and not mention the name of the person who performs the action
(c) When it is obvious who performed the action (e.g. teachers), or when we do not want to use a general subject such as 'people' or 'someone'

narr: The passive voice has several important uses in English. First, we use it to move important information to the beginning of the sentence. For example, 'Two men are being questioned by the police' puts the focus on the men rather than the police.

Second, the passive allows us to be impersonal by not mentioning who performs the action. This is particularly useful in scientific or technical writing, such as 'Oil and gas are found beneath the ground or sea,' where the focus is on the resources rather than the finders.
Third, we use the passive when it's obvious who performed the action, like when teachers assign homework, or when we want to avoid using vague subjects like 'people' or 'someone'.
